**The Last Booth**

The letter came in a plain envelope, which is how you know it's bad news. Good news gets a logo. Marisol read it standing at the kitchen counter with her coat still on: effective the first of March, all lanes on the Route 9 corridor would transition to electronic tolling. Her position would be eliminated. Thank you for twenty-three years of service.

Twenty-three years. She did the arithmetic the way you touch a bruise. Nights, mostly. Ten to six. She'd taken the shift when Danny was small because it meant she could be home when he woke up, and then she'd kept it after he grew and left because by then she couldn't sleep at normal hours anyway. Her body had rearranged itself around the booth.

People assume it's a lonely job. It isn't, exactly. It's the opposite of lonely in a way that's hard to explain. Every ninety seconds, a face. A hand extending out of a window, sometimes with a coin, sometimes with a story. She'd been handed wedding invitations. Baby photos. Once, a man at three in the morning gave her a sandwich, wrapped in wax paper, and said his wife had made too many and he couldn't stand to throw it out. He drove off before she could say anything. She ate it. Turkey and mustard. She still thought about it.

The booth itself was six feet by four. A stool. A heater that worked when it felt like it. A drawer for the cash, a small television she wasn't supposed to have, a radio she was. Over the years she'd added a cushion, a photograph of Danny at his graduation, a plant that had died and been replaced four times. She knew every sound the highway made. She could tell you the difference between a semi carrying a full load and one running empty by the way the pavement hummed before it arrived.

What she would miss, she decided in those last weeks, was the fifteen seconds.

That's about how long a transaction takes. The car slows. The window comes down. Money changes hands. In that gap, something happens that doesn't happen anywhere else. Two strangers who will never see each other again look directly at one another with nothing to sell and nothing to prove. Some people don't look—they hold the money out and stare at the road—and that's fine too, that's its own kind of honesty. But most people look. Most people say something. *Cold one tonight. You have a good one. Long way to Albany still?*

She had learned to read the fifteen seconds. She could tell who was driving toward something and who was driving away. The man in the gray sedan every Tuesday at 1:40 a.m., always alone, always with the radio off—she never asked, and he never offered, but she knew. The young couple who came through in a U-Haul and both said *thank you* at the same time and then laughed at themselves. The woman who paid with quarters, counted out slowly, and apologized, and Marisol said *take your time, honey* and meant it more than she'd meant most things that year.

The new system would be faster. She understood that. A gantry over the road, a camera reading plates, a bill in the mail. No slowing down. No window. She didn't resent the machines. They weren't wrong. They just didn't know what they were replacing, and nobody had thought to tell them.

On the last night, she brought a thermos of coffee and a box of the good pastries from Reyes Bakery and set them on the ledge for anyone who wanted one. Most people didn't notice. A few did. A trucker took a guava pastry and said, "They're really closing you down, huh," and she said yes, and he said, "That's a damn shame," and then, after a second, "I've been coming through here since '09. You always looked like you were doing okay." She didn't know what to do with that, so she just said thank you, and he nodded and pulled away, and his taillights joined the others going north.

Around four the traffic thinned to almost nothing. That was the hour she'd always liked best—the road empty and shining under the sodium lights, the sky not yet doing anything, the sense of being the only person awake in a wide, quiet machine. She turned the radio down. She counted the drawer even though it didn't matter anymore. She looked at the photograph of Danny and thought about calling him, then remembered the time and didn't.

At 5:52 a minivan came through. Woman driving, two kids asleep in the back, their heads tilted toward each other like they'd been arranged. The woman held out a five and said, "Sorry, I don't have anything smaller."

"That's alright," Marisol said, and made change, and then—because it was the last one, and because she'd never once said it in twenty-three years—she added, "Drive safe. You've got precious cargo."

The woman glanced in the rearview mirror at her children. Her face did something. "I do," she said. "Thank you."

Fifteen seconds. Then the window went up and the van moved on and Marisol watched it until the road curved and took it.

At six her relief didn't come, because there was no relief. She turned off the heater. She unplugged the radio. She left the plant, because it was doing well this time and she didn't want to jinx it. She took the photograph and the cushion and the empty pastry box and stood outside the booth for a minute in the cold, looking at the gantry they'd already built, its cameras pointed patiently at nothing.

Then she got in her car and drove home under it, and it read her plate, and didn't say a word.
